question: Format this: Her name was Sasha. Though we had gone to high school together, we were from two different crowds and never really knew each other. We ended up sharing a few classes together our first year of college, and that's when we began to talk. After sitting next to me in one of our classes, she noticed how smart I was and would often ask me for help with anything she didn't understand. Next thing I knew she was sitting next to me in every class we had together. I couldn't believe my luck. I had a major crush on her back in high school, but never had the balls to talk to her. Now she was asking me to spend more time with her outside of class to help tutor her, and I couldn't have been happier to do so. I love getting so much one on one time with her. She was super sweet, completely different from the popular mean girl persona she had in high school. She was always so giggly around me and always finding excuses to put her hands on my arm or shoulder. I couldn't help but feel she was flirting with me, but I still didn't have the nerve to ask her out. We maintained our friendship for the whole year. She would often drag me out to major parties that I never would've been invited to and always did her best to try to include me in conversations and pull me out of my shell a little. She never made any major moves to solidify whether or not she was in to me or just saw me as a really good friend. It got to a point where almost every time we hung out I was waiting for her to say something about how I feel like a brother to her or something, but that never happened. She just continued to confuse me and feed me mixed signals. Summer came along and we parted ways with a hug, and she said she couldn't wait to see me again at the end of summer break, so that felt somewhat promising. I spent all summer thinking about her, missing all the time that I had grown used to spending with her. I watched summer tik away slowly as I impatiently waited for school to start back up again. When the first day of the new year started I saw Sasha quickly making her way towards me. "Oh my God!" She yelled happily. "I'm so glad you're back! The summer was kinda boring without my cute little pet by my side!" Pet.. I wasn't sure how to take that. She did say I was cute.. What kind of message was she trying to give here? I brushed it off and gave her a big hug. We went off to find a quiet spot and she told me all about her summer and how she wished I could've been there with her. Our relationship was starting to feel like it was in a better place than when summer started. Near the end of October she told me that there was going to be this killer costume party and she wanted me to go with her. She was going as a witch and asked if I would be her peasant slave. I thought it was a weird request, but at the same time, this was sounding very much like a couples costume. At this point I had already developed very strong feeling for her and would do whatever it took for an opportunity to win her over, so I happily agreed. The night of the party she came to pick me up. The party was a decent ways off campus, tucked away in the middle of nowhere, so as to avoid cops coming to shut down the party. I was pretty excited. She made for one hot witch, and I didn't care if my costume was kind of demeaning because it made her so happy that we could go together. When we got there I noticed that there weren't a lot of familiar faces, but the party was bumpin either way so I didn't care nor think much of it. As the night carried on she drug me around with her everywhere, showing off our costumes, often joking about how she planned on taking me back to her lair for her dinner. She kept handing me beer after beer, I assumed trying to get me to loosen up. I'm not the most social person ever and can get kind of shy in groups. Her plan was working however. The more I drank the easier it was to open up and enjoy myself. It had started getting late and a lot of people had already made their way home. There were still a few stragglers, ourselves included. She took me by the hand and led me into a big empty room. She turned to look at me and grabbed me by the hand. "You've been a good little peasant slave," she said with a giggle and a wink. "Now, being the generous witch that I am, I'll grant you one free wish! What'll it be!?" I was heavily intoxicated, and as I looked at her gorgeous face, only one thing came to mind. "I just want to be yours forever." As soon as I said it I froze up. I hadn't thought before I spoke, and now it was all out there. I guess now I would finally get my definitive answer. A smile formed on her black lips. "What would you do to prove that you're worthy to be mine?" Was she serious? Did I actually stand a chance!? "I would do anything your heart desires," I said as sweetly as my drunken self could muster. She reached into her purse and pulled out salt and a candle. I was confused but just watched as she made a ring of salt on the floor and lit the candle in the middle of it. "I will give you the ultimate test then," she said stepping out of the circle after lighting the candle. "Step inside the circle." I did as she said and she started to mumble words I couldn't understand.

question: Byline: Nazish Imran, Aateqa Hashmi and Ahad Imran KEYWORDS: Artificial Intelligence, Child Mental Health, ChatGPT, Open AI, Mental Illness. "ChatGPT puts the power of AI in everyone's hand." - Fredrick Godin ChatGPT is making a significant impact in everyone's life around the globe, including younger population. More than 25% of the population of the world is under the age of 14. Mental Health in children and adolescents is a pressing public health issue. The World Health Organization estimates that nearly 20% of these children suffer from psychiatric problems.1 With huge treatment gap in Child and adolescent mental health care especially in low and middle-income countries and increase need for psychiatric diagnosis and treatment services, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital interfaces are emerging as viable alternatives for reducing this gap. The ChatGPT (Chat-Generative Pre-Trained Transformer) and other AI-based chatbot's ability to generate human-quality responses can help in making mental health services accessible and affordable.2 Chat-GPT is an AI-based language model which uses natural language processing (NLP) and conversational AI to help mental health professionals deliver more personalized and effective mental health support. This is possible because the system is powered by a machine learning algorithm, trained using large dataset of clinical interactions in healthcare. ChatGPT can support child and adolescent mental health by supporting physicians as well as patients and families in various ways. Benefits for Mental Health Practitioners: A resource for Mental health clinicians: ChatGPT could be used to analyze a child and adolescent's language text for patterns and correlations that can reveal underlying mental health issues. It can help clinicians in providing quick access to assessment tools, new evidence-based treatment options and best clinical practices for managing common child and adolescent mental health problems. It can also flag potential drug interactions and help in reducing prescription errors, while saving clinician's time.3 Enhance Proactive treatment adjustments: ChatGPT can assess intensity of negative cognitive distortions by analyzing patients' language patterns in real time, which alongside clues from mental health state examination may help clinicians to improve diagnostic accuracy, determine early treatment response and enhance proactive adjustments in treatment.4,5 Extracting Information from Large sets of Data: Chat GPT can use its vast database of language to generate reports and summaries from large sets of data, such as patient interviews. This could assist mental health practitioners to diagnose children and adolescents and develop personalized treatments quickly and accurately. Lab reports, imaging results and any other relevant information can also be extracted quickly from patients records.5 Facilitation of Communication: ChatGPT can facilitate communication between young patients and mental health professionals by precise and swift translation of medical jargon and technical terminologies due to its advanced language processing capabilities. It thus allows clinicians to help engage children and adolescents in their management plan and better understand their diagnosis and treatment options. Integration of ChatGPT enabled apps in healthcare devices: ChatGPT enabled apps and its potential integration in healthcare devices such as smart wearables, and other monitoring devices is one of the most exciting developments and can have a potential future role in offering real time insight in child and adolescent health status . Teaching and Training in child mental health: ChatGPT can be effective tool in medical education, Child and adolescent mental health teaching and training by identifying gaps in knowledge, for content creation, producing high quality engaging content at scale, helping in lesson planning and assessments.6 This can be very cost effective in improving awareness of child and adolescent mental health amongst schoolteachers and allied pediatric health professionals. reference: The table provides data on various studies conducted to evaluate the prevalence of comorbidities in individuals with spinal cord injuries (SCI) in Iran. The studies included in the table have investigated a wide range of comorbidities such as depression, anxiety, sexual dysfunction, bone mineral density, respiratory function, and biochemical androgen deficiency, among others. The studies have employed different study designs, such as cross-sectional studies, retrospective studies, systematic literature reviews, and prospective studies. Data collection methods have also varied across the studies, including questionnaires, medical record reviews, and laboratory tests. The findings of the studies highlight the high prevalence of comorbidities among individuals with SCI in Iran. For example, depression and anxiety were found to be common psychological side effects of SCI, and sexual dysfunction was found to be highly prevalent among Iranian women with SCI. Reduced bone mineral density was also observed, which was more severe in femoral bone sites and higher reduction of lumbar BMD was shown when the level of injury was above T6. In addition, the studies found that veterans with SCI were at risk for pressure area ulcers, reactions to severe stress and adjustment disorders, diabetes mellitus, and kidney and/or urologic disorders. The prevalence of obesity and overweight was shown to be lower among patients with SCI compared to the general Iranian population, although older patients had higher BMIs. The studies suggest that the management of comorbidities should be an integral part of SCI care in Iran. question: System analysis by David Easton
reference: David Easton developed the concept of system analysis in the field of political science. System analysis refers to the study of political systems and their components, such as institutions, actors, and processes, in order to understand how they function and interact with each other. Easton's system analysis framework is based on the idea that political systems can be understood as a set of inputs, conversion processes, and outputs. Inputs refer to the demands, support, and resources that are brought into the political system by various actors and groups. Conversion processes involve the transformation of these inputs into policy decisions and actions by political institutions and actors. Finally, outputs are the outcomes and consequences of these policy decisions and actions. According to Easton, system analysis helps in understanding the functioning of political systems by focusing on the interrelationships between different components and the ways in which they contribute to the overall stability and effectiveness of the system. He also emphasized the role of feedback mechanisms in maintaining the equilibrium of political systems. Easton's system analysis has been widely applied in the study of various political phenomena, such as policy-making, decision-making processes, and the role of different actors in the political system. It has provided a useful framework for analyzing the complex and dynamic nature of political systems and has helped in identifying the factors that shape political outcomes. Overall, David Easton's system analysis has made significant contributions to the field of political science by providing a systematic approach to understanding political systems and their functioning. This guidance is structured under several key considerations: ### 1. **Local Zoning and Housing Laws** - **Short-term Rental Regulations:** Some cities have specific regulations regarding short-term rentals, which can include limits on the number of days you can rent out a property or require certain standards to be met. - **Change of Use Permit:** Depending on the zoning laws, you might need to apply for a change of use for the property from residential to commercial if the authorities consider short-term renting a commercial activity. ### 2. **Registration and Licenses** - **Business Registration:** You may need to register as a business, depending on how much income you generate or the frequency of your rentals. - **Tourist Accommodation License:** In some jurisdictions, properties listed on short-term rental sites must obtain a license or permit indicating they meet specific safety and health standards. ### 3. **Taxation** - **Income Tax:** Income generated from renting your property must be reported to the Slovak tax authorities, and you'll be taxed accordingly. - **Local Taxes:** Besides income tax, be aware of any local taxes or tourist taxes that may apply to short-term rentals. ### 4. **Insurance** - **Liability Insurance:** It's advisable to have liability insurance to protect against potential claims from guests. - **Property Insurance:** Insurance companies often require a different type of coverage for properties being rented out short-term versus those used exclusively by the owner. ### 5. **Safety and Health Regulations** - Making sure your property complies with local safety standards (like smoke detectors, emergency exits, etc.) and health regulations is crucial to avoid penalties. ### 6. **Building and Homeowners' Association Rules** - If your studio is in a building or area governed by an association, you'll need to check if there are any restrictions on short-term rentals. ### 7. **Neighborhood Considerations** - Be mindful of your neighbors and consider implementing measures to prevent noise or disturbances, which could lead to complaints or legal issues. ### 8. **Data Protection Laws** - When dealing with guests' personal information, ensure you comply with the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) standards. ### Final Recommendations: - **Legal and Tax Advice:** Consult a lawyer and a tax professional who specialize in property rental and short-term accommodation in Slovakia. - **Local Authorities:** Contact the local municipality and tax office in Trenčín for specific requirements and advice. question: Andretti Company has a single product called a Dak. The company normally produces and sells 80,000 Daks each year at a selling price of $62 per unit. The company’s unit costs at this level of activity are given below: Direct materials $ 7.50 Direct labor 9.00 Variable manufacturing overhead 2.60 Fixed manufacturing overhead 8.00 ($640,000 total) Variable selling expenses 3.70 Fixed selling expenses 4.50 ($360,000 total) Total cost per unit $ 35.30 A number of questions relating to the production and sale of Daks follow. Each question is independent. Required: 1-a. Assume that Andretti Company has sufficient capacity to produce 108,000 Daks each year without any increase in fixed manufacturing overhead costs. The company could increase its unit sales by 35% above the present 80,000 units each year if it were willing to increase the fixed selling expenses by $110,000. What is the financial advantage (disadvantage) of investing an additional $110,000 in fixed selling expenses?
reference: To evaluate the financial advantage or disadvantage of investing an additional $110,000 in fixed selling expenses to increase unit sales by 35%, we'll calculate the increase in profit that would result from the increase in sales and then subtract the additional fixed selling expenses. ### Current Situation: - Annual Sales: 80,000 Daks - Selling Price per Dak: $62 - Total Sales Revenue: $62 * 80,000 = $4,960,000 - Variable Cost per Unit: $7.50 (materials) + $9.00 (labor) + $2.60 (variable manufacturing overhead) + $3.70 (variable selling expense) = $22.80 - Total Variable Cost: $22.80 * 80,000 = $1,824,000 ### Fixed Costs: - Fixed Manufacturing Overhead: $640,000 - Fixed Selling Expenses: $360,000 - Total Fixed Costs: $640,000 + $360,000 = $1,000,000 ### Profit Calculation (Current Situation): - Total Cost (Variable + Fixed): $1,824,000 + $1,000,000 = $2,824,000 - Profit: $4,960,000 (Revenue) - $2,824,000 (Total Cost) = $2,136,000 ### New Situation With Increased Sales: - Increased Sales by 35%: 80,000 * 1.35 = 108,000 Daks - Additional Fixed Selling Expenses: $110,000 ### New Sales and Profit: - New Total Sales Revenue: $62 * 108,000 = $6,696,000 - New Total Variable Cost: $22.80 * 108,000 = $2,462,400 - New Total Fixed Costs: $640,000 (Manufacturing) + $360,000 (Selling) + $110,000 (Additional Selling) = $1,110,000 ### New Profit Calculation: - New Total Cost (Variable + Fixed): $2,462,400 + $1,110,000 = $3,572,400 - New Profit: $6,696,000 (Revenue) - $3,572,400 (Total Cost) = $3,123,600 ### Financial Advantage/Disadvantage: - Increase in Profit = New Profit - Old Profit = $3,123,600 - $2,136,000 = $987,600 By incurring an additional $110,000 in fixed selling expenses to increase sales, Andretti Company stands to increase its profit by $987,600, which demonstrates a significant financial advantage.

question: We have conducted a survey of political activism among college students in Pennsylvania, and 73% of the survey’s 100 respondents stated that they have volunteered for a political campaign in the past. If a leading political theorist has hypothesized that 45% of college students have volunteered for a political campaign in the past, can we reject that hypothesis at the .05 significance level? Group of answer choices Yes No
reference: To determine whether we can reject the hypothesis that 45% of college students have volunteered for a political campaign in the past, we can conduct a hypothesis test. Let's set up the null and alternative hypotheses: Null hypothesis (H0): The proportion of college students who have volunteered for a political campaign in the past is 45%. Alternative hypothesis (H1): The proportion of college students who have volunteered for a political campaign in the past is not 45%. Now, we can perform a one-sample proportion test using the sample data: Sample proportion (p̂) = 73% = 0.73 Sample size (n) = 100 Under the null hypothesis, assuming that the proportion is 45%, we can calculate the expected number of students who have volunteered for a political campaign as (0.45 * 100) = 45. The test statistic for a one-sample proportion test is given by: z = (p̂ - p) / sqrt(p(1-p)/n) Substituting the values: z = (0.73 - 0.45) / sqrt(0.45 * 0.55 / 100) Using a standard normal distribution table or calculator, we can find the critical z-value for a 2-tailed test at a significance level of 0.05. The critical z-value is approximately ±1.96. Comparing the calculated test statistic to the critical z-value, if the calculated test statistic exceeds the critical z-value (in absolute value), we can reject the null hypothesis. Calculating the test statistic: z = (0.73 - 0.45) / sqrt(0.45 * 0.55 / 100) = 0.28 / sqrt(0.2475 / 100) = 0.28 / 0.04975 = 5.63 (rounded) Since the calculated test statistic (5.63) exceeds the critical z-value (±1.96) in absolute value, we can reject the null hypothesis. Therefore, at the 0.05 significance level, we can reject the hypothesis that 45% of college students have volunteered for a political campaign in the past.

question: make the following better: "Into to Credit Rover The purpose of credit rover is to systematically search the IG market for relative value ideas and flag them to PMs/traders/analysts who can apply their judgement to filter further for actionable ideas. It is a tool designed to enable FIG to generate new sources of alpha within the funds, a one-stop shop for Relative Value (RV) - for PMs, Credit analysts and Traders, a centralized warehouse for all the data needed to make investment decisions, and a common place for Research and Trading to signal trade ideas and discuss them. Credit Rover is part of a bigger platform called the Insights Platform. It aims to enable efficient market insights through intelligent data aggregation, interactive modules, and configurable alerts. Over time, the Insights platform should expand to support additional applications, especially given the volume of proprietary information we have—which grows every day. RV & Signal RV stands for Relative Value. It is a quantitative analytical approach and is a systematic way to address the fundamental question: what’s expensive and what’s cheap? It allows us to identify relative misvaluations between and among securities, and if they improve the quality of the predictions we make about the future richening and cheapening of these securities. Credit RoVer uses mainly price adjusted OAS to generate relative value signals. The aim is to have one centralized place for all data RV everyone would agree upon. Curve fitting is needed as the starting point for relative value. It allows us to judge which bonds are cheap or rich on an issuer's curve, as well as generate a long history of 5y, 10y, 30y, etc. points to make apples to apples comparisons across issuers for the purpose of relative value. In RoVer, what we effectively try to do is fit thousands of curves automatically and every day. Each issuer or benchmark has a specific curve. Not time efficient to build it out manually for each of them. Curve fitting can be used as an aid for data visualization (term structure), to infer values of a function where no data is available (new issues), and to summarize the relationship among two or more variables (maturity and model OAS). What we effectively do here is generate signals for the desk that help them narrow down potential opportunities to capture alpha. In RoVer, all signals have mean reversion as an underpinning assumption. There are two types of signals, one is spread/standard RV, which focus on CUSIP vs curve signal; the other is regression RV, which illustrates curve vs curve signal. Both signals are generated based on price adjusted OAS. Spread RV looks at distance of latest value of a specific point w.r.t. mean of that same point over a specific window. Each CUSIP has 10 different options of benchmark curves, either issuer curve, or 9 other benchmarks consisting of combination of sector and ratings. This method is typically used on the Bond Selection Page. For example, the graph below looks at AAPL CUSIPs against AAPL issuer curve. The spread to curve (STC) is called the residual. We then take all STC/residuals from AAPL and find their mean. The RV signal/z-score is expressed is expressed in number of standard deviations away from mean. If the latest value is below mean, spread is considered expensive, and the RV signal is negative. If above mean, spread is considered cheap, and the RV signal is positive. Always with mean reversion as a base case. Regression RV look at how the spread of a specific point on a fitted curve compares with the same point on the benchmark curve historically. This method is shown under ‘RV Z Score’ on the Issuer Selection and Forecasting page. Taking AAPL as an example, the spread between the AAPL issuer curve and the Technology A and Above curve is the spread to benchmark (STB). We take all STB and find their mean. If latest point of STB is trading below the mean (negative RV signal), it’s considered expensive (positive RV signal). Conversely, when above the mean it is considered cheap. Both Spread and Regression RV signals have different options of look-back window, meaning the signal is built based on 10 days, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years of historical data. Back-testing The underpinning assumption of the RV signals is that all signals follow mean reversion. For back-testing, we want to see if the underpinning assumption holds in different regions. We want to evaluate if the spread is moving in the same direction or not as indicated by the RV signal. Let’s assume we choose look-back window of 3 months and expect the mean-reversion happens in 30 days (holding period = 30 days). As shown in the graph below. If the current CUSIP is trading at px adj OAS of 100 bps, while it’s issuer curve (after curve fitting) at the same tenor shows 90 bps of px adj OAS, it means that the CUSIP is currently trading cheap relative to its issuer curve. If the signal of this CUSIP has a RV z-score of 1, which means that this CUSIP is currently trading at 1 stdev above the 3 months historical STC mean. If we hold this CUSIP for 30 days (expect the mean-reversion happens in 30 days), if the RV signal is the right indication, we are expecting it to be mean reverted, which means that the STC should becomes smaller regardless of the CUSIP or the IC moves. At T + 30, both scenarios shown in the graph on the right-hand side follow mean reversion, where we are expecting this CUSIP to become rich. Likewise, the opposite scenario exhibits a divergent dynamic. To perform a thorough back-testing, we tested RV signals with all available look-back periods that the signals are based on, 10 days, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years. We are expecting the signals to be mean reverted, but mean reversion can happen at different time frame. So we look at different holding periods to see how mean reversion occurs, at 2 weeks, 1 month, 2 months, 3 months, and 6 months, which can also be extended in the future as needed. In addition, to better understand the performance of RV signals, we performed bucket analysis on RV signals as well as maturities of the bonds. Bin the signals in buckets of (-Inf, -3.0], (-3.0, -2.5], (-2.5, -2.0], …, (2.5, 3.0], (3.0, Inf], and maturity (yrs) in buckets of 0-3, 3-5, 5-7, 7-10, 10-15, 15-20, 20-30, 30+. For the back-testing results discussed below, we are testing with 2 years of historical data from 2020-2022. And we breakdown the analysis by currency as well. The results above show the statistics of the residual (STC) movement of CUSIPs in the format of average, median, standard deviation, and P-value. To be more specific, on the far right, we can specify currency, RV signal look-back window, maturity bucket, and historical dates. In this case, we are looking at USD with look-back window of 90 days (3 months). To better understand what the result means, if we look at the upper left cell, where RV z-score bucket is in (3, Inf) with a holding period of 2 weeks, it means that for all bonds in the historical testing data with z-score of 3 and above, on average, residual (STC) tightened 5.79 bps over 2 weeks of holding period. It indicates mean reversion preserves for this specific z-score bucket with this holding period, as positive z-score indicates that the bonds are currently trading cheap (above the mean) and expected to become rich (expensive – smaller px adj oas) over time. From the result, we can see that the monotonical increasing in the residual movements (bps) with the decreasing in the z-score buckets, which indicate overall mean reversion occurs in this scenario. The stronger the signals are, the larger residual movements occurred. A small p-values give stronger support statistically. We also look at how hit rate performs over holding periods by buckets over time. The graph above shows the daily average hit rate of CUSIPs that exhibited residual change in right direction over the holding period. Similarly, we find that the stronger the signals are (more stdev away from the mean), the higher the hit rates are over time. Throughout the back-testing, we’ve found that RV signals strongly follow mean reversion in USD, with different look-back windows and holding periods. The longer the look-back window (2yr) as well as the holding period (6 months), the stronger the signals are. CAD also tends to follow mean reversion, but not as strong as USD. For European and Australian market (EUR, GBP, AUD), mean reversion is minimally from the observation. The main reason is that the bulk of EUR and GBP issuers have very few debts outstanding, and as a result, the curves fitted are less reliable compared with USD. The quant team is working on improving the curve fitting for the next step. Additional highlight on OAS Analysis Apart from back testing the RV signals, we did analysis on OAS in addition to the residual (STC). The reason behind it is that we want to have a better understanding of the market overall. We’ve noticed that the average daily OAS movement is monotonically increasing with the decreasing of RV z-score during 2020-2022. This indicates that rich bonds cheapen more than cheap bonds over time. The yields on rich bonds are increasing at a faster rate than the yields on cheap bonds. This OAS analysis gives us a better understanding of the impact of beta with given period. We have the back-testing results built into the Tableau report, and plan to have it refreshed quarterly to keep track of the behavior of RV signals. On top of that, the report also has a version to select by issuers based on need"

question: System analysis by David Easton
reference: David Easton developed the concept of system analysis in the field of political science. System analysis refers to the study of political systems and their components, such as institutions, actors, and processes, in order to understand how they function and interact with each other. Easton's system analysis framework is based on the idea that political systems can be understood as a set of inputs, conversion processes, and outputs. Inputs refer to the demands, support, and resources that are brought into the political system by various actors and groups. Conversion processes involve the transformation of these inputs into policy decisions and actions by political institutions and actors. Finally, outputs are the outcomes and consequences of these policy decisions and actions. According to Easton, system analysis helps in understanding the functioning of political systems by focusing on the interrelationships between different components and the ways in which they contribute to the overall stability and effectiveness of the system. He also emphasized the role of feedback mechanisms in maintaining the equilibrium of political systems. Easton's system analysis has been widely applied in the study of various political phenomena, such as policy-making, decision-making processes, and the role of different actors in the political system. It has provided a useful framework for analyzing the complex and dynamic nature of political systems and has helped in identifying the factors that shape political outcomes. Overall, David Easton's system analysis has made significant contributions to the field of political science by providing a systematic approach to understanding political systems and their functioning. It has helped researchers and analysts to gain insights into the complexities of politics and to develop theories and models for explaining political behavior and outcomes.

Avoid repeating words or Ideas "In her 1984 essay, “Under Western Eyes: Feminist Scholarship and Colonial Discourses,” postcolonial feminist scholar Chandra Talpade Mohanty put forth a scathing critique – not just of Western feminist scholarship, but also the ways in which it tends to oversimplify and stereotype the experiences of women in the Global South (Mohanty 337). Mohanty’s central point is that Western feminists should avoid constructing monolithic categories of “the third-world woman,” as such a characterization only perpetuates colonial discourses (Mohanty 342). She identifies six dominant feminist discourses that contribute to the portrayal of “Third World women” as a unified and homogenous group. These discourses depict “Third World women” as victims of male violence, colonial oppression, family systems, development processes, and religious ideologies. These representations often position “Third World women” as passive and vulnerable, lacking agency and independence."
reference: In her 1984 exposition, "Under Western Eyes: Feminist Scholarship and Colonial Discourses," Chandra Talpade Mohanty, a prominent postcolonial feminist theorist, vehemently scrutinizes Western feminist academia and its tendency to simplify and caricature the experiences of women hailing from the Global South (Mohanty 337). Mohanty primarily asserts that it is imperative for Western feminists to eschew the formulation of monolithic classifications of "the third-world woman," since such characterizations serve to further entrench colonial dialogues (Mohanty 342). Mohanty discerns six prevailing feminist discourses that contribute to the depiction of "Third World women" as an amalgamated and homogenized collective. These discourses portray these women as casualties of masculine brutality, colonial subjugation, familial structures, developmental machinations, and religious dogmatism. Consequently, these representations frequently posit "Third World women" as both passive and susceptible, devoid of the capacity to exercise agency and autonomy.

question: 1. What would your vision and expectations be if you were the Manager of our new Biggleswade Branch, short and long term? Feel free to include such points as turnover, number of staff, types of customer and anything else that you feel is relevant.
reference: As the Manager of the new Biggleswade Branch, my vision and expectations would be centered around establishing a successful and thriving branch that contributes significantly to the overall growth and profitability of the organization. Here are my short and long-term goals: Short-term: 1. Establish a strong foundation: Prioritize building a robust infrastructure and efficient processes to ensure smooth operations from the beginning. 2. Recruitment and training: Assemble a talented and motivated team, ensuring they are equipped with the necessary skills and knowledge to effectively serve our customers. 3. Customer acquisition: Focus on attracting a diverse range of customers from different demographics and industries. Develop marketing strategies, including local advertising and community engagement, to increase brand awareness and drive traffic to the branch. 4. High-quality service: Emphasize exceptional customer service to build trust and loyalty. Regularly review customer feedback and make necessary improvements to meet or exceed their expectations. 5. Financial performance: Strive for profitability by closely monitoring key financial indicators, optimizing expenses, and setting realistic short-term targets. Long-term: 1. Sustainable growth: Expand our customer base and increase market share by offering innovative products and services tailored to local needs. 2. Employee development: Foster a culture of continuous learning and career advancement. Provide regular training and growth opportunities to nurture a motivated and skilled workforce. 3. Branch expansion: Evaluate opportunities for expanding the branch's physical footprint based on market demand and performance. Consider opening additional branches in adjacent areas to strengthen our regional presence. 4. Profitability: Aim for steady revenue growth and a strong return on investment. Implement effective cost management strategies while maintaining high-quality service. 5. Community involvement: Establish a positive reputation within the local community by actively participating in social initiatives and supporting local organizations. In terms of specific metrics, my expectations for the Biggleswade Branch would include: - Achieving a targeted turnover growth rate of, for example, 15% annually. - Building a team of skilled professionals, starting with a core staff of approximately 10 employees, and expanding as necessary to meet customer demand. - Attracting a diverse customer base, including individuals, small businesses, and corporate clients, to ensure a balanced portfolio and reduce dependency on a single segment. - Maintaining high customer satisfaction scores, with a target of 90% or above. - Building long-term relationships with customers, leading to increased cross-selling opportunities and customer retention. Ultimately, my vision for the Biggleswade Branch is to establish it as a trusted and successful entity within the community, recognized for its outstanding service, strong financial performance, and contributions to the overall success of the organization.

Дополнительные указания: Избегайте использования плагиата или перефразирования с помощью синонимайзеров, Стремитесь к созданию уникального и оригинального текста, который не будет идентичен исходному, Ни одно предложение из созданного вами не должно точь-в-точь повторять исходное, уберите из текста весь мусор вроде ссылок. Разбей текст на абзацы. Заголовок для текста придумывать не нужно. Вот сам текст: Editors' notes This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked trusted source proofread Using waste to purify water may sound counterintuitive. But at TU Wien, this is exactly what has now been achieved. Researchers have developed a special nanostructure to filter a widespread class of harmful dyes from water. A crucial component is a material that is considered waste: used cellulose, for example in the form of cleaning cloths or paper cups. The cellulose is utilized to coat a fine nano-fabric to create an efficient filter for polluted water. The paper is published in the journal Small Science. Organic dyes represent the largest group of synthetic dyes, including so-called azo compounds. They are widely used in the textile industry, even in countries where little attention is paid to environmental protection, and the dyes often end up in unfiltered wastewater. "This is dangerous because such dyes degrade very slowly, they can remain in the water for a long time and pose great danger to humans and nature," says Prof. Günther Rupprechter from the Institute of Materials Chemistry at TU Wien. There are various materials that can bind such dyes. But that alone is not enough. "If you simply let the polluted water flow over a filter film that can bind dyes, the cleaning effect is low," explains Rupprechter. "It's much better to create a nanofabric out of lots of tiny fibers and let the water seep through." The water then comes into contact with a much larger surface area, and thus many more organic dye molecules can be bound. "We are working with semi-crystalline nanocellulose, which can be produced from waste material," says Qaisar Maqbool, first author of the study and postdoc in Rupprechter's research group. "Metal-containing substances are often used for similar purposes. Our material, on the other hand, is completely harmless to the environment, and we can also produce it by upcycling waste paper." This nano-cellulose is "spun" together with the plastic polyacrylonitrile into nanostructures. However, this requires a lot of technical skill. The team from the TU Wien was successful with a so-called electrospinning process. In this process, the material is sprayed in liquid form, the droplets are electrically charged and sent through an electric field. "This ensures that the liquid forms extremely fine threads with a diameter of 180 to 200 nanometers during curing," says Rupprechter. These threads form a fine tissue with a high surface area—a so-called "nanoweb." A network of threads can be placed on one square centimeter, with a total surface area of more than 10 cm2. The tests with these cellulose-coated nanostructures were very successful: In three cycles, water contaminated with violet dye was purified, and 95% of the dye was removed. "The dyes remain stored in the nanoweb. You can then either dispose of the entire web or regenerate it, dissolve the stored dyes and reuse the filter fabric," explains Rupprechter. However, more work needs to be done: evaluating the mechanical properties of the sophisticated nanowebs, conducting biocompatibility tests, assessing sensitivity to more complex pollutants, and achieving scalability to industrial-grade standards. Now Rupprechter and his research team want to investigate how this dye filter technology can be transferred to other areas of application. "This technology could also be very interesting for the medical field," Rupprechter believes. "Dialysis, for example, also needs filtering out very specific chemical substances from a liquid." Coated nanofabrics may be useful for such applications. More information: Qaisar Maqbool et al, Waste‐Valorized Nanowebs for Crystal Violet Removal from Water, Small Science (2024). DOI: 10.1002/smsc.202300286 Provided by Vienna University of Technology
reference: В сфере научных исследований в Венском технологическом университете (TU Wien) произошел прорыв, позволяющий смотреть на отходы под совершенно новым углом. Ученые разработали уникальную наноструктуру, способную фильтровать воду от вредных красителей, для создания которой используется материал, традиционно считающийся отходом – использованная целлюлоза. Такие предметы, как тряпки для уборки или бумажные стаканчики, обретают новую жизнь, превращаясь в эффективный фильтр для загрязненной воды. Исследование было опубликовано в престижном журнале Small Science. Органические красители, особенно азосоединения, составляют большую группу синтетических красителей, широко используемых в текстильной промышленности. К сожалению, они часто попадают в сточные воды без предварительной очистки, особенно в странах с низким уровнем экологической ответственности. Эти вещества медленно разлагаются и могут долгое время оставаться в воде, представляя серьезную угрозу для здоровья человека и окружающей среды. Как отмечает профессор Гюнтер Руппрехтер из Института химии материалов TU Wien, само по себе использование материалов, способных адсорбировать такие красители, недостаточно эффективно. Гораздо лучше работает метод, при котором вода пропускается через наноткань, состоящую из мельчайших волокон. Это увеличивает площадь контакта и позволяет связать гораздо больше молекул красителя. Используемый материал, полу-кристаллическая наноцеллюлоза, получают из отходов, предотвращая их ненужную утилизацию. И в отличие от металлосодержащих веществ, применяемых для похожих целей, она абсолютно безопасна для окружающей среды. Технология электропрядения, при которой жидкий материал распыляется, а его капли электрически заряжаются и проходят через электрическое поле, позволяет получать сверхтонкие нити. Так формируется наноткань – наносеть с высокой площадью поверхности. Испытания показали впечатляющие результаты: за три цикла очистки удавалось удалять до 95% красителя из воды. Наносеть можно либо безопасно утилизировать с захваченными вредными веществами, либо регенерировать, очищая от красителей для повторного использования. Несмотря на успех, перед учеными стоят новые задачи – исследовать механические свойства наносети, оценить ее биосовместимость, чувствительность к более сложным загрязнителям и возможности масштабирования производства. Команда профессора Руппрехтера теперь изучает, как технологию фильтрации красителей можно применить в других областях, например, в медицинской индустрии для очистки жидкостей при диализе. Такие покрытые наноткани могут найти широкое применение в новых, инновационных областях.

question: //I wanted to change AutoRedirect per request using the same HttpClient. //But this is not possible because it throws an exception: This instance has already started one or more requests. Properties can only be modified before sending the first request. //Here is my solution, Please let me know if you have any notes or optimizations //Usage: var handler = HttpClientHelper.CreateHttpHandler(); var client = HttpClientHelper.CreateHttpClient(handler); //redirects to https var url = "http://stackoverflow.com/"; //AllowAutoRedirect = true var content = await HttpClientHelper.SendAsync(client, url, autoRedirect: true).ConfigureAwait(false); //AllowAutoRedirect = false content = await HttpClientHelper.SendAsync(client, url, autoRedirect: false).ConfigureAwait(false); //Class public static class HttpClientHelper { public const string UserAgent = "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/110.0.0.0 Safari/537.36"; private const string AutoRedirectPropertyKey = "RequestAutoRedirect"; private static readonly HttpRequestOptionsKey<bool?> AutoRedirectOptionsKey; public static CustomHttpClient CreateHttpClient(HttpMessageHandler handler, bool disposeHandler = true) { var client = new CustomHttpClient(handler, disposeHandler); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd(UserAgent); return client; } public static HttpClientHandler CreateHttpHandler(bool autoRedirect = true) { return new HttpClientHandler { AllowAutoRedirect = autoRedirect }; } public static void SetAutoRedirect(this HttpRequestMessage request, bool autoRedirect) { if (request == null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(request)); request.Options.Set(AutoRedirectOptionsKey, autoRedirect); } public static bool? GetAutoRedirect(this HttpRequestMessage request) { if (request == null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(request)); return request.Options.TryGetValue(AutoRedirectOptionsKey, out var value) ? value : default; } public static Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(CustomHttpClient client, string url, bool autoRedirect = true) { var uri = new Uri(url); var request = new HttpRequestMessage { RequestUri = uri, Method = HttpMethod.Get }; request.SetAutoRedirect(autoRedirect); return client.SendAsync(request); } public static HttpMessageHandler? GetMostInnerHandler(this HttpMessageHandler? self) { while (self is DelegatingHandler handler) { self = handler.InnerHandler; } return self; } } public class CustomHttpClient : HttpClient { public CustomHttpDelegate HandlerWrapper; public CustomHttpClient(HttpMessageHandler handler, bool disposeHandler = true) : this(new CustomHttpDelegate(handler), disposeHandler) { } private CustomHttpClient(CustomHttpDelegate handler, bool disposeHandler = true) : base(handler, disposeHandler) { HandlerWrapper = handler; } } public class CustomHttpDelegate : DelegatingHandler { private int MaxAutomaticRedirections { get; set; } private bool InitialAutoRedirect { get; set; } private readonly HttpMessageHandler? _mostInnerHandler; private readonly ExpiringDictionary<HttpRequestMessage, bool?> _customAutoRedirectDic = new(); public CustomHttpDelegate(HttpMessageHandler innerHandler) : base(innerHandler) { _mostInnerHandler = innerHandler.GetMostInnerHandler(); SetupCustomAutoRedirect(); } private void SetupCustomAutoRedirect() { try { switch (_mostInnerHandler) { case HttpClientHandler hch: InitialAutoRedirect = hch.AllowAutoRedirect; MaxAutomaticRedirections = hch.MaxAutomaticRedirections; hch.AllowAutoRedirect = false; break; case SocketsHttpHandler shh: InitialAutoRedirect = shh.AllowAutoRedirect; MaxAutomaticRedirections = shh.MaxAutomaticRedirections; shh.AllowAutoRedirect = false; break; default: Debug.WriteLine("[GetAndTurnOffAutoRedirect] Unknown handler type: {0}", _mostInnerHandler?.GetType().FullName); InitialAutoRedirect = true; MaxAutomaticRedirections = 17; break; } } catch (Exception e) { Debug.WriteLine(e.Message); InitialAutoRedirect = true; MaxAutomaticRedirections = 17; } } private bool IsRedirectAllowed(HttpRequestMessage request) { var value = request.GetAutoRedirect(); if (value == null) return InitialAutoRedirect; return value == true; } protected override async Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { var redirectCount = 0; var response = await base.SendAsync(request, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false); //Manual Redirect Uri? redirectUri; while (IsRedirect(response) && (redirectUri = GetUriForRedirect(request.RequestUri!, response)) != null && IsRedirectAllowed(request)) { redirectCount++; if (redirectCount > MaxAutomaticRedirections) break; response.Dispose(); // Clear the authorization header. request.Headers.Authorization = null; // Set up for the redirect request.RequestUri = redirectUri; if (RequestRequiresForceGet(response.StatusCode, request.Method)) { request.Method = HttpMethod.Get; request.Content = null; if (request.Headers.TransferEncodingChunked == true) { request.Headers.TransferEncodingChunked = false; } } // Issue the redirected request. response = await base.SendAsync(request, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false); } return response; } private bool IsRedirect(HttpResponseMessage response) { switch (response.StatusCode) { case HttpStatusCode.MultipleChoices: case HttpStatusCode.Moved: case HttpStatusCode.Found: case HttpStatusCode.SeeOther: case HttpStatusCode.TemporaryRedirect: case HttpStatusCode.PermanentRedirect: return true; default: return false; } } private static Uri? GetUriForRedirect(Uri requestUri, HttpResponseMessage response) { var location = response.Headers.Location; if (location == null) { return null; } // Ensure the redirect location is an absolute URI. if (!location.IsAbsoluteUri) { location = new Uri(requestUri, location); } // Per https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-7.1.2, a redirect location without a // fragment should inherit the fragment from the original URI. var requestFragment = requestUri.Fragment; if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(requestFragment)) { var redirectFragment = location.Fragment; if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(redirectFragment)) { location = new UriBuilder(location) { Fragment = requestFragment }.Uri; } } return location; } private static bool RequestRequiresForceGet(HttpStatusCode statusCode, HttpMethod requestMethod) { switch (statusCode) { case HttpStatusCode.Moved: case HttpStatusCode.Found: case HttpStatusCode.MultipleChoices: return requestMethod == HttpMethod.Post; case HttpStatusCode.SeeOther: return requestMethod != HttpMethod.Get && requestMethod != HttpMethod.Head; default: return false; } } }

The use of a delegating handler and the separation of concerns among different methods in the `HttpClientHelper` class effectively handles the issue you were facing. Ensure you handle exceptions appropriately, as certain sections of the code may throw exceptions that are not currently being accounted for. 4. Add more XML comments to the code to provide better inline documentation for the different methods and classes. Overall, your solution effectively addresses the problem at hand, and with a few improvements to thread safety and error handling, it will be a solid implementation.

question: Story prompt: 13-year-old Max was headed to a friend’s house. As someone who can’t drive yet, he uses a ride-sharing app to get from one place to another. On this day, however, he ended up sharing a ride with a stranger. 13 years old as well, she was dressed fashionably and had an air of popularity to her. Someone who definitely went out with friends more often than others. According to the app, her destination was a large shopping mall, closer than Max’s friend’s house, thought pretty far away. It would take about 30 minutes to get to the mall. In the meantime, Max, who was never one to initiate conversation, kept to himself. Still, 30 minutes was gonna take a while. “So… mall, huh?”, awkwardly asked Max to start a conversation. “Yeah.”, was the response she gave him. Doesn’t seem like she was interested. Why would she? Everyone’s a stranger in the car. This was gonna be a long ride. Still, it didn’t seem like she was completely cold and distant. After a few minutes had passed, Max opened up with, “Hanging out with a friend today. Thinking you’re doing the same?” The girl responded, “Yeah. Probably just gonna go window shopping.”, while on her phone. “Got any other plans after that?”, asked Max. Even she was surprised to answer him so casually, saying, “We got basketball practice today at 4.” Max replied, “Oh, cool. I had a feeling you were the sporty type too.” It didn’t take long for the seemingly awkward boy and the seemingly disinterested girl to actually engage in long conversations. It didn’t even register to them that they were already at the mall. “I’m Max, by the way.” The girl replied, “My name’s Suzanna. Or Suzie, but whatever. It was nice talkin’ to you, Max.”, just before closing the door and going inside the mall. As the car began to head to his friend’s house, Max couldn’t help but think to himself, “I just had a good conversation with a stranger. Pretty, too.”
reference: As Max watched Suzanna disappear into the bustling crowd at the entrance of the mall, a small grin spread across his face. He couldn’t help but chuckle inwardly, realizing just how odd it was for him to strike up a conversation like that, and even odder that he enjoyed it. Delighted by the unexpected interaction, Max settled back into the car seat, his initial unease evaporating. The remainder of the ride felt shorter than he expected. Max was lost in thought, analyzing every part of the conversation, wondering if maybe he had seemed too curious, too eager, or just plain awkward. Yet, something about Suzanna’s casual demeanor felt refreshing. He wasn't used to this—making a connection so effortlessly. Max's friend greeted him with a wave from the front porch as the car pulled up to the curb. After thanking the driver, he hopped out and jogged up to the house, all the while recounting the ride to his waiting friend. Dusk approached as Max and his friend wrapped up a day filled with video games and laughter. While walking home, Max's thoughts wandered back to Suzanna. The way she talked about basketball practice with such passion, how she switched from a detached stranger to an engaging conversationalist—it sparked something within Max, a newfound confidence that maybe he could be that person, too. From that day on, Max no longer dreaded the ride-sharing trips to his friend's house or back home. He found himself more open to chatting with drivers or passengers, and his circle of acquaintances started to grow. At school, he became less of the quiet kid in the corner and more of the friendly face in the crowd, even striking up a conversation with a few of Suzanna's friends who recognized him from the ride share. As fate would have it, several weeks later, Max found himself in the same car with Suzanna once more. This time, the conversation started instantly, as if they were old friends catching up. They shared a laugh over the coincidence of their paths crossing again in such a busy city. “Looks like the universe has a weird sense of humor, huh?” Max said with an easy smile, as the car pulled away, blending into the city’s traffic. Suzanna grinned back. “I guess it does, Max. Maybe this should be a regular thing, shared ride buddies?” Max’s heart skipped a beat, not just at the suggestion, but at the realization that simple twists of fate could lead to such unexpected friendships, and maybe, in time, to even more.

Competency codes integration: - Incorporate IET competency codes into the application, making it possible for users to link their reports to relevant competencies. Once you have designed and implemented the application, consider deploying it to a hosting service such as Heroku, Netlify, or Digital Ocean. question: Summarize this paragraph:The ecological diversity of the KSA allows multiple opportunities for the evolution of variation in both mosquitoes and their pathogens. Large-scale movements of people, including the annual pilgrimage to Mecca, large-scale use of foreign workers and new developmental projects engender environmental heterogeneity and complex epidemiology. The wide variation in ecological settings may complicate the understanding of spatial/temporal characteristics and population dynamics of mosquito vectors of pathogens that cause diseases in humans. Investigators may be reluctant to conduct ecological studies in the KSA because field work is labour-intensive and time-consuming. Moreover, due to habitat heterogeneity, which in the KSA is often extreme, there are species of only seven mosquito genera in the country. Here we present the first complete list (see above) of the mosquito species that definitely are known to occur in the KSA. In some cases, ecological and morphological studies have shown that some species are members of species complexes. There are members of four Anopheles species complexes in the country, including the An. gambiae, An. fluviatilis, An. culicifacies and An. subpictus complexes. The Afrotropical An. gambiae complex consists of eight species, which includes malaria vectors (An. gambiae, An. arabiensis, An. bwambae, An. coluzzii, An. merus and An. melas) and non-vectors (An. quadriannulatus and An. amharicus) [70, 71]. Anopheles arabiensis is the only member of the complex with a range that extends outside of Africa into the southwestern and western areas of the Arabian Peninsula, occurring in the KSA and Yemen, where it is the major malaria vector [2, 3, 7, 72,73,74,75]. Most ecological studies conducted in the KSA recorded the presence of An. arabiensis (often as An. gambiae) in different life stages [27, 29, 30, 51]. Moreover, molecular analysis based on the internal transcribed spacer (ITS2) region of rDNA has shown that An. arabiensis (GenBank: KM068071) is the only member of An. gambiae complex present in the KSA [59]. The An. fluviatilis complex is a group of mosquitoes that is widely distributed in southern and southwestern Asia and includes important malaria vectors [76]. The complex includes four species informally denoted as species S, T, U and V [77,78,79,80,81]. Anopheles fluviatilis S is mainly anthropophilic, endophilic and a very competent malaria vector [52]. Species T and U are primarily zoophilic, exophagic and exophilic, and are regarded as poor- or non-vectors of malaria even though they are responsible for malaria transmission in mountainous and hilly areas in Asia, including Iran [80, 82]. Anopheles fluviatilis (s.l.) was recorded in the eastern and western regions of the KSA by Mattingly & Knight [2], Wills et al. [31] and Al-Ghamdi et al. [51]. It is not known whether species T or U or both are present in the KSA. The An. culicifacies complex consists of five sibling species, informally named species A, B, C, D and E, based on cytotaxonomic and molecular evidence [53, 76, 83]. These species have distinct geographical distributions, blood-feeding behaviour and vectorial capacity for malaria transmission [54, 84, 85]. The complex is widely distributed from southern China to Iran, the Arabian Peninsula and Ethiopia [86]. Species E is the most important malaria vector in the Indian subcontinent, and is highly anthropophilic and endophilic [87]. The other sibling species have low anthropophilic index or are highly zoophilic, and are considered poor- or non-malaria vectors in India and Sri Lanka [52, 88]. Available data indicate there are at least two species of the complex in Iran [89], but only the presence of species A has been confirmed based on cytogenetic and molecular evidence; the second species may be a new member of the complex [90]. Further study is needed to determine which member or members of the complex are present in the KSA. The An. subpictus complex consists of four species in India, informally denoted as species A, B, C and D, based on morphological, chromosomal and molecular differences [91, 92]. As is the case in Iran [90], it is not known which species of the complex is present in the KSA. Anopheles stephensi is the main malaria vector in the eastern region of the KSA, but members of the An. fluviatilis and An. culicifacies complexes, which are important malaria vectors in other parts of Asia [2, 3, 55, 74], may contribute to malaria transmission. In Asia, An. stephensi, An. culicifacies (s.l.) and An. fluviatilis (s.l.) consist of different ecoforms that are restricted to rural or urban areas with different degrees of involvement in malaria transmission [54, 76, 85]. Anopheles stephensi is a major vector in Asia and the Middle East, including, in addition to the eastern KSA, areas of Iran, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India and southern China [87]. It includes three ecological variants (egg phenotypes): the mysorensis, typical and intermediate forms, which are based and distinguished on egg morphology [87, 93,94,95,96]. The typical (type) form is mainly found in urban areas, whereas the intermediate and mysorensis forms are mainly found in rural environments [87]. The blood-feeding behaviour and role of these forms in malaria transmission varies in different geographical regions. In Iran, the type form is highly anthropophilic and a major malaria vector, whereas the mysorensis form is mainly zoophilic and a poor- or non-vector [97]. In contrast, the mysorensis form is an important malaria vector in India [98]. These differences might be due to the type of host available and the presence of certain mosquito genotypes with different host preference and susceptibility to malarial parasites. Molecular study using two different markers (ITS2 and cox1) did not reveal any differences between An. stephensi (ITS2, GenBank: KM052589; and cox1, GenBank: KJ528887–KJ528894) in two distant cities of the KSA (Al-Ahsaa and Dammam) where different phenotypes might be present [59]. Anopheles azaniae was first encountered in Saudi Arabia during the collection of mosquitoes for Rift Valley virus isolation in the Jizan Region [17], and subsequently collected in the same region by Alahmed et al. [18] and Khater et al. [7]. The record of this species in the Riyadh Region [32], which is a very large eastern region that shares its southern border with Yemen, requires confirmation. The record of this species in the more northerly western Al-Madinah Al-Munawarah Region [33] is doubtful and a probable misidentification of either An. dthali or An. rhodesiensis rupicolus. Anopheles azaniae was previously known to occur in neighbouring Yemen [14], where two morphological forms were recently discovered, the typical form and a previously unrecognized form not immediately identifiable as An. azaniae [99]. A single specimen of the atypical form had a mixed human/bovine blood meal, indicating that females are anthropophilic and should be considered a potential vector of malarial protozoa. It seems possible that further studies in the southwest of the KSA may detect the presence of the atypical form. A species of the genus Coquillettidia collected in the Eastern Province of the KSA was identified as a species of Mansonia in the study of Wills et al. [31]. According to the online catalogue of the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit [24], only two species of the tribe Mansoniini are known to occur in more or less arid countries of the Middle East, Cq. (Coquillettidia) buxtoni in Israel and Syria and Cq. (Coq.) richiardii in Iran, Syria and Turkey. With that in mind, it seems likely that the generic identification of Wills et al. [31] was based on keys available at the time, e.g. Mattingly [100], which treated Coquillettidia as a subgenus of Mansonia. In view of the proximity of eastern areas of the KSA to Iran, we are confident that the mosquitoes identified as a species of Mansonia by Wills et al. [31] were most likely specimens of Cq. richiardii. Many of the occurrence records for Cx. pipiens and Cx. quinquefasciatus in the KSA are problematic. Culex pipiens generally occurs north of a line transecting the KSA between Jeddah in the west and Al-Hasa in the east. Culex quinquefasciatus occurs in the more southerly region of the Arabian Peninsula, with isolated populations of Cx. pipiens occurring in the southwestern mountains [5]. Introgression occurs between the two species where their distributions overlap in central KSA (see figure 3 in Harbach [101]). Both species exhibit considerable variation in the larval and adult stages, and they cannot always be distinguished with certainty. They are only reliably distinguished by characters of the male genitalia; however, their separation is complicated by the occurrence of hybrid forms in the central transitional zone and eastern coastal region of the country. Hybrids are morphologically more variable than the parental species, and are only reliably distinguished from the parental species by the DV/D ratio calculated from measurements based on the form and relationships of the dorsal and ventral arms of the male genitalia [102, 103]. It is not possible to distinguish hybrid larvae and females from the parental species. For this reason, some hybrid specimens collected in and around the zone of introgression have undoubtedly been misidentified as either Cx. pipiens or Cx. quinquefasciatus. Larvae and adults collected north of the hybrid zone that have been identified as Cx. quinquefasciatus are misidentified specimens of Cx. pipiens, and those collected south of the zone that have been identified as Cx. pipiens, with the possible exception of those collected in the southwestern mountains, are misidentified specimens of Cx. quinquefasciatus. Future studies based on dissections of male genitalia or DNA sequence analysis of larvae and adults are needed to substantiate species identifications and collection records. Culex quinquefasciatus is an important vector of the microfilariae that cause lymphatic filariasis. Culex torrentium is listed as a species of the KSA in the online catalogue of the Walter Reed Biosystematics Unit [24] based on a number of reports, including Alahmed et al. [18, 19], Al Ahmed et al. [20, 28], Kheir et al. [34], Alahmed [35] and Hassan et al. [41]. However, it is obvious that the identification of Cx. torrentium in the KSA by these authors is based on unreliable characters of larvae and adult habitus principally using the keys of Harbach [4, 5]. This species can only be distinguished from members of the Cx. pipiens complex with certainty based on features of the male genitalia. Additionally, Cx. torrentium is a Palaearctic species whose distribution only extends south into Turkey and possibly into northern Iran [90, 104, 105]. As noted by Harbach [5], early records of Cx. torrentium in Iraq are doubtful, and the species is not now listed as present in that country [106, 107]. For these reasons, Cx. torrentium is excluded from the list of mosquito species known to occur in the KSA. Four species of the subgenus Culex of the genus Culex occur in the southwestern Afrotropical Region of the Arabian Peninsula, i.e. Cx. decens, Cx. duttoni, Cx. simpsoni and Cx. univittatus. These species were only known to occur in Yemen [5, 108] until they were more recently found in the Asir Region [63], Jizan (Jazan) Region [18] and Najran Province [28], which border Yemen in the southwest corner of the KSA. The records of two of these species, Cx. simpsoni and Cx. univittatus, require confirmation because their identification was based on larvae and adults. They are only reliably distinguished from Cx. sinaiticus and Cx. perexiguus, respectively, based on the morphology of the male genitalia. Records of the two species in more northerly areas of the country are more doubtful. Since Culex salisburiensis has been known to be present in Yemen since 1953 [108], there is no reason to doubt its occurrence in the adjacent Afrotropical area of the KSA [21, 67]. On the contrary, the reported finding of Cx. wigglesworthi in the Asir Region by Al Ashry et al. [67] is certainly a misidentification. The authors collected 4307 Culex larvae, two of which were identified as Cx. nebulosus, three as Cx. perexiguus and two as Cx. wigglesworthi. Larvae were identified using the keys of Hopkins [109], Mattingly & Knight [2] and Harbach [4, 5]. The identification of Cx. nebulosus and Cx. perexiguus may be correct as these two species are included in the keys of Mattingly & Knight (Cx. nebulosus) and Harbach (Cx. nebulosus and Cx. perexiguus). Use of the badly outdated keys of Hopkins [109] for African species published in 1952, leading to the identification of Cx. wigglesworthi, is problematic, nonetheless because it is a sub-Sharan species with closest records in southern Sudan, South Sudan and Kenya. Consequently, as it seems likely that the two larvae were misidentified specimens of either Cx. perexiguus or Cx. univittatus, Cx. wigglesworthi is excluded from the list of mosquito species known to occur in the KSA. Alahmed [35], Alahmed et al. [36] and Khater et al. [7] recorded the presence of Uranotaenia (Pseudoficalbia) unguiculata in eastern and southwestern areas of the KSA. The authors, however, were apparently unaware of the earlier description of Ur. unguiculata pefflyi by Stone [69], and the recognized presence of only that form in eastern parts of the KSA [31]. Consequently, as it is unlikely that the typical form, Ur. unguiculata unguiculata, is present in the country, only the subspecies described and named by Stone [69] is included in the list.

Both species exhibit considerable variation in the larval and adult stages, and they cannot always be distinguished with certainty. They are only reliably distinguished by characters of the male genitalia; however, their separation is complicated by the occurrence of hybrid forms in the central transitional zone and eastern coastal region of the country. Hybrids are morphologically more variable than the parental species, and are only reliably distinguished from the parental species by the DV/D ratio calculated from measurements based on the form and relationships of the dorsal and ventral arms of the male genitalia [102, 103]. It is not possible to distinguish hybrid larvae and females from the parental species. For this reason, some hybrid specimens collected in and around the zone of introgression have undoubtedly been misidentified as either Cx. pipiens or Cx. quinquefasciatus. Larvae and adults collected north of the hybrid zone that have been identified as Cx. quinquefasciatus are misidentified specimens of Cx. pipiens, and those collected south of the zone that have been identified as Cx. pipiens, with the possible exception of those collected in the southwestern mountains, are misidentified specimens of Cx. quinquefasciatus. Future studies based on dissections of male genitalia or DNA sequence analysis of larvae and adults are needed to substantiate species identifications and collection records. Culex quinquefasciatus is an important vector of the microfilariae that cause lymphatic filariasis. However, it is obvious that the identification of Cx. torrentium in the KSA by these authors is based on unreliable characters of larvae and adult habitus principally using the keys of Harbach [4, 5]. This species can only be distinguished from members of the Cx. pipiens complex with certainty based on features of the male genitalia. Additionally, Cx. torrentium is a Palaearctic species whose distribution only extends south into [REDACTED] and possibly into northern [REDACTED] [90, 104, 105]. As noted by Harbach [5], early records of Cx. torrentium in [REDACTED] are doubtful, and the species is not now listed as present in that country [106, 107]. For these reasons, Cx. torrentium is excluded from the list of mosquito species known to occur in the KSA. Four species of the subgenus Culex of the genus Culex occur in the southwestern Afrotropical Region of the Arabian Peninsula, i.e. Cx. decens, Cx. duttoni, Cx. simpsoni and Cx. univittatus. These species were only known to occur in [REDACTED] [5, 108] until they were more recently found in the Asir Region [63], Jizan (Jazan) Region [18] and Najran Province [28], which border [REDACTED] in the southwest corner of the KSA. Records of the two species in more northerly areas of the country are more doubtful. Since Culex salisburiensis has been known to be present in [REDACTED] since 1953 [108], there is no reason to doubt its occurrence in the adjacent Afrotropical area of the KSA [21, 67].
